verses.translation_literal: Of David. To you, YHWH, my soul I lift up.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David. Everything I am, I lift up to you, O LORD, and I hold it out in both hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The opening line sets the pose for the whole poem: the speaker raises his nefesh, his throat, his appetite, his life, toward God. Nefesh is not the 'soul' of later Greek thought, a ghost inside a body. It is the neck and breath and craving of a living person, so the gesture is closer to a hungry man looking up than to a monk's meditation. The word order matters: 'to you' comes first, before the name, and the verb comes last, so every hearer waits for the thing lifted.

The KJV gets the sense, with 'do I lift up' added to fill out the English. It also splits off 'A Psalm of David' as a separate verse 0, as if it were a title with its own number; the Hebrew has 'Of David' as the first word of the verse. The traditional commentators disagree on what the lifting means: a gesture of prayer (Radak, comparing Lam 3:41), an offering (Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion, comparing Gen 43:34), or the longing of a hired worker waiting for his pay (Ibn Ezra, comparing Deut 24:15). The actor need not choose; the posture of reaching upward fits all three.

philological_notes.note: Nefesh is the whole living self: throat, breath, appetite. 'My soul' in English is a pale substitute. Here it is the thing that is lifted, so the line says that the speaker offers his life and his longing.
'I lift up'. The same verb is used of lifting hands in prayer, of carrying a gift, and of a worker lifting his soul toward his wage. The commentaries split on which of those pictures is meant.

verses.translation_literal: My God, in you I have trusted; may I not be ashamed; may my enemies not exult over me.
verses.translation_dramatic: My God, I have put my weight on you. Do not let me be left red-faced, and do not let my enemies crow over me.
verses.directors_commentary:
In the ancient Near East shame was a public event: a man who staked his name on a patron or an ally and was let down stood exposed before his neighbours. To trust in God was to bet one's reputation on him, and to be 'ashamed' was to lose that bet where everyone could see. The enemies in the second half are the audience waiting for that fall. The verb 'exult' (alatz) is a loud, physical verb of celebration, a victory shout.

The KJV 'let me not be ashamed' is right, though 'let not mine enemies triumph over me' makes it sound like a battle; the Hebrew is the joy of onlookers, not necessarily a military victory. The poem is an alphabetic acrostic, and the letter bet that ought to begin this verse sits instead on the word בְּךָ, 'in you', the second word, so the line starts with aleph again (Radak and Meiri discuss the missing letters). An actor can use that: the word 'in you' lands as the first thing the speaker really stands on.

philological_notes.note: 'I have trusted'. A perfect verb of reliance: leaning one's full weight on something and finding that it holds. It is not a vague hope; it is a deed already done, which is the ground for the plea that follows.
Shame here is public disgrace, the opposite of vindication. The lengthened cohortative form marks a strong wish: 'may I never be ashamed'.

verses.translation_literal: Also all who wait for you will not be ashamed; they will be ashamed, the treacherous ones, emptily.
verses.translation_dramatic: And not only I. No one who waits for you will ever be shamed. Let the shame fall on the faithless, the ones who betray for nothing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker widens his plea: it is not only his own face at stake but that of everyone who waits for God. The verb qavah, 'to wait', also means 'to hope' and has the image of a cord pulled tight, so waiting is tension, not idleness. The verse turns on one repeated word, 'be ashamed': first denied to those who wait, then handed to the treacherous. Say it twice, with the weight shifting.

The last word, reikam, 'emptily', is the one the KJV smooths as 'without cause'. It can mean for nothing, with no reason (Ibn Ezra: 'for free'; Metzudat Zion) or, as Rashi reads it, 'empty-handed', and the same word in Ps 7:5. The people are the faithless, those who betray without any provocation. The KJV's 'transgress' is too moral and too small for bogedim, which are treacherous dealers, the people who break faith in a relationship. The first line in the KJV, 'Yea, let none', also turns a statement of fact into a wish; the Hebrew has a plain future, 'they will not be ashamed'.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who wait for you'. The participle of the verb that also means to hope. The speaker counts himself among them, and it is repeated in v5 as 'I have waited for you'.
'Emptily', 'for nothing'. Ibn Ezra reads the final mem as a surplus ending on the word for 'for free'. Rashi reads it as 'empty-handed': the treacherous dealers send the poor away with nothing.

verses.translation_literal: Your ways, YHWH, make known to me; your paths teach me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Show me the way you walk, O LORD. Teach me the paths that are yours.
verses.directors_commentary:
A pair of parallel lines, 'ways' and 'paths', 'make known' and 'teach'. Both objects are placed first, so the speaker begins with what he wants and only then names the verb. The petition is not for directions to a destination but for a way of living that is God's own: his conduct, his habits.

The KJV's 'shew me' and 'paths' are fine, though 'shew' is archaic. Both Radak and Meiri treat the two lines as one idea in different words, and Radak compares Moses' request in Exod 33:13, 'make me know your ways'. Malbim finds a difference: derekh is the broad road, orach the narrow side-track that needs more teaching. The Hebrew can bear either, and the director may let the actor lean into the second.

philological_notes.note: 'Your ways'. A derekh is a trodden road and also a manner of life. The same root gives the verb 'lead' in v5 and v9, so the poem keeps returning to the road.
'Your paths'. Malbim distinguishes it from derekh as a branching track off the main road; that is his reading and not a settled lexical difference.

verses.translation_literal: Make me tread in your truth, and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation; you I have waited for all the day.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lead me, step by step, along your truth, and teach me. You are the God who saves me, and I have waited for you the whole day long.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Make me tread' is a causative: the verb darakh means to step on, to tread a road, and the causative form is the guide who takes the learner by the hand, as Radak says, like a man leading a child until he can walk alone. The speaker asks to be walked along God's truth, emet, which in Hebrew is reliability, what holds up under weight, more than a set of true facts. The second verb, 'teach', is 'and teach me': the vav, the missing acrostic letter, is tucked in mid-verse here and not at the head of a line (Radak and Meiri on the acrostic).

The last two lines give the reason and the waiting. 'God of my salvation' is the title the speaker bets on. Then the object marker comes first, 'you I have waited for', so the emphasis is on you and no one else. 'All the day' is a plain phrase for continually (Radak), though Rashi reads 'day' as this present world, which is day for the nations and night for Israel. The KJV 'on thee do I wait' is sound, though it hides that the verb is the same qavah as v3. BBE's 'your word' is invented: the Hebrew says 'you'.

philological_notes.note: Causative of 'tread': 'make me walk'. Radak explains it as leading a child little by little until the child walks on his own.
'Truth' in the sense of what is firm and dependable, reliability. The same word joins 'chesed' in v10.
'I have waited', 'I have hoped'. It is the verb behind 'those who wait for you' in v3, so the speaker joins the group he spoke of.

verses.translation_literal: Remember your compassion, YHWH, and your covenant loyalties, for from of old they [are].
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember your mercies, O LORD, and your faithful love. They are not new; they are as old as time.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Remember' in Hebrew is an act, not a memory: when God remembers, he acts. The speaker asks God to act on two qualities that he names in the plural: rachamim, which comes from rechem, the womb, so it is the tenderness of a mother for her child, and chasadim, the loyalty owed inside a covenant. The reason he gives is that these have always been there, 'from of old', so it would be out of character for God to stop now. This is an argument from God's own record.

The KJV's 'tender mercies' for rachamim is good, and 'lovingkindnesses' for chasadim is a clumsy plural but keeps the sense, whereas YLT's 'kindnesses' loses the covenant. The phrase 'from of old' is me'olam, and olam means an unmeasured long time. Rashi takes it back to Adam and the thousand-year day. Radak takes it to the speaker's own life, from the womb on. The director should keep it open and let the line speak as 'as long as anyone can remember'.

philological_notes.note: 'Remember', in the sense of 'act on'. The speaker uses it twice more in v7 with opposite requests, remember what is good and do not remember the sins.
'Your compassion', from the root of the word for womb: a parent's tender feeling.
'Your covenant loyalties': acts of faithful love that fulfil a bond. The plural suggests many repeated deeds.

verses.translation_literal: [The] sins of my youth and my transgressions do not remember; according to your covenant loyalty remember me, you, for the sake of your goodness, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not remember the sins of my young years, or my rebellions. Remember me as your own faithful love would remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb 'remember' now turns round. In v6 God is asked to remember his mercies; here he is asked not to remember the speaker's wrongs. The line sets two kinds of memory against each other, and the speaker puts God in the position of choosing which to keep. The pairing 'sins' and 'transgressions' is not an accident. Radak and Meiri take chata'ot as the unwitting or immature wrongs of youth, and pesha' as deliberate rebellion, the breaking away from an authority one knows. That is their reading; the words do overlap in other places.

The KJV 'according to thy mercy remember thou me' is fine, but 'mercy' stands for chesed, which is covenant loyalty, not pity. The little word 'attah', 'you', stands alone and emphatic near the end: 'remember me, you'. It marks the contrast between the speaker's record and God's own character. The final phrase 'for the sake of your goodness' is exactly that; BBE's 'righteousness' is not what tuv means. The speaker asks to be judged not by what he has done but by what God is like.

philological_notes.note: 'My youth', a plural of abstraction, the stage of life from boyhood to early adulthood.
'My transgressions', literally acts of rebellion against an authority. Radak and Meiri contrast it with chata'ot.
'According to your covenant loyalty': the measure by which the speaker asks to be remembered.

verses.translation_literal: Good and upright [is] YHWH; therefore he teaches sinners in the way.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is good and he is straight. That is why he shows sinners the road.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone changes. The speaker has been asking; now he states a fact about God, and the fact is the reason for everything he has asked. 'Good' and 'upright' are two qualities in one breath: goodness, which is generous, and uprightness, which is straight and fair. The consequence is surprising: because God is straight, he teaches sinners. A modern audience expects the opposite.

The Hebrew has no 'will' in 'will he teach'; the verb is a plain present, yoreh, 'he teaches', which is a habit, not a future promise. The KJV and ASV add 'will'. The verb yarah gives the word Torah, so 'he teaches' is of the same root as 'instruction'. Rashi reads the sinners as those who return in repentance; Radak sees the way as the way of return, taught since Cain (Gen 4:7). Rashi's second reading, murderers sent along the road to a city of refuge (Deut 19:3), is a midrashic one, and the actor can safely ignore it.

philological_notes.note: 'He teaches', 'he instructs'; literally 'he points the way', the root of Torah.
'Sinners', literally 'those who miss the mark'. It is a different noun from the 'sins' of v7 but from the same root.

verses.translation_literal: He makes the humble tread in justice, and he teaches the humble his way.
verses.translation_dramatic: He walks the humble along the path of what is right, and to those same humble he teaches his own way.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two halves repeat 'the humble', anavim, and the repetition is the point: the people who are taught are the ones who know they need teaching. Anav is not the soft, weak 'meek' of English; it is someone who does not push himself forward, who bends to correction. The verbs echo v4 and v5, 'tread' and 'teach', so the answer to the speaker's prayer arrives in the vocabulary of the prayer.

The KJV 'in judgment' for ba-mishpat is misleading for a modern ear, which hears a courtroom verdict. The word is justice in the sense of the right way of ordering things. BBE's 'poor in spirit' leans on the overlap of anav with ani, 'poor', but the word here is the humble. Radak reads the humble as those who have turned from sin and the 'justice' as the known law; Malbim as those who know the road but are held back by need. The director may play the line as plain comfort.

philological_notes.note: 'The humble': those who bow, who do not claim a place for themselves. It is close to ani, 'poor', and the two are sometimes confused, but the word here is the humble.
'Justice', 'the right order'. Here it is a way of living and not a court decision.

verses.translation_literal: All [the] paths of YHWH [are] covenant loyalty and faithfulness, for those who keep his covenant and his testimonies.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every road the LORD walks is faithful love and truth, for those who keep his covenant and heed what he has testified.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'paths' from v4 return, and now they are described: all of them are chesed and emet, covenant loyalty and faithfulness. This is the most compact statement of what God is like in the Hebrew Bible, and the speaker has been using the two words throughout the poem. They are the paired terms of Exod 34:6, though the psalm does not quote it. The qualification at the end matters: the paths are loyalty and faithfulness for those who keep the covenant. It is the bond between two parties.

The KJV's 'mercy and truth' puts chesed as 'mercy', which makes it a matter of pity, while chesed is about loyalty to a bond. 'Testimonies', edot, are the commands and signs by which God bears witness to himself, a covenant document. 'Keep' is nazar, to guard as one guards a treasure. Ibn Ezra relates 'keepers of the covenant' to Exod 34:7, 'keeping loyalty for thousands', and Malbim holds that even the paths that look harsh are an expression of one of the two. The director should take the verse as a creed spoken slowly.

philological_notes.note: 'Covenant loyalty and faithfulness': a paired formula of God's steadfast character. The first is the commitment, the second the reliability of carrying it out.
'Those who keep': the verb is to guard, to watch over, which suggests care and not only obedience.
'His testimonies': the commands and signs that bear witness to the covenant.

verses.translation_literal: For the sake of your name, YHWH, and you will forgive my iniquity, for it [is] great.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the sake of your name, O LORD, forgive my guilt. It is great.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the creed of v10, the personal plea returns, and it is startling. The speaker does not argue that his guilt is small. He says it is great, and uses that as the reason: only a God whose name is forgiveness can deal with a debt this size. 'Name' in the Hebrew world is reputation and character; to act 'for the sake of your name' is to appeal to who God is, not to what the speaker deserves. The verse starts with lamed, the next letter in the acrostic.

The KJV 'pardon' is good, and the 'for' joining the last clause is the same Hebrew ki. The grammar is a request in the form of a promise: 'and you will forgive', which carries the force of 'forgive!'; YLT turns it into a past statement, which misreads it. The word avon, 'iniquity', is the crookedness and the guilt that follows it; it is singular, 'my iniquity', and Radak and Meiri see a specific deed (Bathsheba), but the text does not say so. Rashi reads 'for it is great' as a reason: it befits the great God to forgive a great sin. Ibn Ezra and Meiri take it as 'although it is great'. Both readings work; play the line without deciding.

philological_notes.note: 'For the sake of your name': an appeal to God's own reputation and character as the ground of forgiveness.
'And you will forgive'. The verb salach is used only of God; a prayer for pardon in the weqatal, with the force of a request.
'For it is great'. Rashi reads it as 'because it is great'; Ibn Ezra and Meiri read 'although it is great'.

verses.translation_literal: Who [is] this, the man fearing YHWH? He will teach him in [the] way [that] he chooses.
verses.translation_dramatic: Who is he, then, this one who fears the LORD? Look for him. The LORD himself will teach him, and set his feet on the road that he has chosen.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here from the speaker's own plea to a question put to the room: 'Who is this man?' Play it as an open invitation, not a riddle. The answer is a promise. Note the verb יוֹרֶנּוּ: from the root that gives Torah, 'instruction' (a teacher pointing the way), so the 'way' is a taught road, not a map handed over.

The last word is ambiguous, and the ambiguity is old. Rashi, Radak and Meiri take God as the subject: the LORD teaches him the way the LORD chooses for him, the good way. Metzudat David, and Ibn Ezra as Radak reports him, take the man as the subject: God teaches him the way the man himself has chosen. The KJV, 'in the way that he shall choose', keeps the ambiguity by luck of English, but its 'him shall he teach' (ASV likewise) leaves two 'he's with no one to tell them apart. BBE settles it flatly for God ('the way of his pleasure') and makes the question disappear. 'Feareth' is archaic; the word is the ordinary Hebrew for awe-struck reverence, closer to 'is in awe of' than to dread.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of a root meaning 'to shoot, to point, to throw' and so 'to direct, to teach'; the noun תּוֹרָה comes from it. The picture is a teacher pointing the way, which suits the 'way' that follows.
'He will choose.' The subject is disputed: God (Rashi, Radak, Meiri) or the man (Metzudat David, Ibn Ezra as cited by Radak).

verses.translation_literal: His soul in good will lodge, and his seed will possess [the] land.
verses.translation_dramatic: That one will lay down his very self each night in goodness, and sleep there untroubled. And his children's children will walk out upon the land and take it as their own.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb תָּלִין is the verb of the night-halt: you lodge somewhere until morning, as a traveller does at an inn. So the picture is of a life that beds down every evening inside good, a settled and unthreatened dwelling. The KJV 'dwell at ease' gets the comfort right but loses the nightly lodging, and the poem has just spoken of roads and ways (verses 4, 8, 9, 12), so a lodging is where the road ends for the day. The word נֶפֶשׁ ('soul') is not a ghost inside the body; it is the whole living person, throat, appetite and self, which is why 'his soul will lodge' just means 'he will rest'.

The second half is the old covenant promise in compact form. In a world where wealth was land and land stayed in the family, 'his seed will possess the land' is the promise of a future for one's name. The KJV 'inherit the earth' stretches אֶרֶץ to the whole planet. The Hebrew word, with no article here, means the land, and a first audience would hear Canaan. Medieval readers (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David) took the lodging as rest in the grave or in the world to come; the plain verse speaks of a good life now.

philological_notes.note: From לוּן, to pass the night, to lodge. It is the verb of the overnight stop, not of permanent dwelling (that would be יָשַׁב). Rashi reads it as the soul lodging in good even in the grave.
Not a detachable soul but the living self; 'his soul' is idiomatic for 'he himself'.

verses.translation_literal: [The] counsel of YHWH [is] for those fearing him, and his covenant, to make [it] known to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD's own counsel is kept for those who fear him: the quiet word spoken among friends. And his covenant? He means them to know it.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a statement about access. סוֹד is the circle of trusted people sitting close together, and what is said inside it; Jeremiah 23:18 and Amos 3:7 use it for the council in which God's plans are shared with his servants. Say 'counsel' as a lowered voice: the in-group at the fire, not a puzzle to be solved. The second half is shorter and more direct, with no verb of its own: 'and his covenant, to make known to them.' It leans on the first half's 'for', so the covenant too is something God means to disclose.

KJV 'The secret of the Lord is with them that fear him' is sound as far as it goes, though 'secret' in modern English suggests something hidden and withheld, where the Hebrew suggests an intimate circle admitted to the confidence. ASV 'friendship' is a stretch: in my own judgement it stretches the sense of an intimate circle into a relationship of friendship, which the word does not itself name. KJV's 'he will shew them' turns the infinitive into a future tense; the Hebrew is an infinitive of purpose, 'to make known to them'. BBE's 'agreement' for בְּרִית is accurate but loses the covenant's weight.

philological_notes.note: A circle of intimates and the confidential talk inside it; 'counsel, council'. Not a hidden thing as such but a shared confidence.
Hiphil infinitive, 'to cause them to know'. It states the purpose or intent of the covenant, not a simple future 'he will show'.

verses.translation_literal: My eyes [are] continually to YHWH, for he [is the one who] brings out my feet from [the] net.
verses.translation_dramatic: My eyes never leave the LORD. I do not look down at the ground where the snare is hidden. I look up, because he is the one who draws my feet out of the net.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker walks a road full of traps, and he keeps his eyes on God instead of the ground. The image is the hunter's net, רֶשֶׁת, a mesh spread on the path to catch a bird or a gazelle by the legs. The foot is caught and cannot move; only someone else can cut it free. The psalmist's confidence is that the one who sets a person free from a net is the one he is already looking at.

The form יוֹצִיא is a participle-like imperfect, 'he is the one who brings out', and so describes God's habit, not a single rescue. The KJV 'he shall pluck my feet' makes it a promise of one future act and adds a verb of violence ('pluck') that the Hebrew lacks; the verb is the plain 'bring out', the same verb used for the Exodus. The net is a favourite image in the Psalms for the enemy's plots (9:15, 31:5, 35:7), though the medieval commentators (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri) also read it as the net of temptation or trouble.

philological_notes.note: A hunter's net spread on the ground to catch the feet. Used in the Psalms for the hidden plot of an enemy.
Hiphil of 'go out': 'make go out', the verb of the Exodus. Not 'pluck'.

verses.translation_literal: Turn to me and show me favor, for [I am] alone and afflicted, I.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn to me. Turn your face my way, and be gracious. For I stand here alone, and bowed down, and no one else is here.
verses.directors_commentary:
פְּנֵה is the plain command 'turn', and the idea is that God turns his face toward the speaker, so that the speaker is finally seen. In Hebrew the face is where favour is shown. חָנֵּנִי is the grace a stronger party gives to someone who has no claim on it; the KJV 'have mercy' is close, but 'mercy' belongs more to רַחֲמִים, and the word here is closer to 'be gracious to me'.

יָחִיד means 'only', as in an only child (Genesis 22:2), and so 'solitary, alone, without family or friends'. The KJV 'desolate' is a guess from context and drops the aloneness. עָנִי is 'poor, bowed down', someone pressed low by others. The two words together describe a man with no backer and no power. Radak and Meiri observe that the speaker is traditionally David the king, and so read 'alone and poor' as humility before God, but nothing in the verse says that; it is the cry of anyone with no one to stand beside them.

philological_notes.note: 'Only, alone'; used of an only child (Genesis 22:2, Judges 11:34) and so of one without kin or support. The KJV 'desolate' is not what the word says.
From ענה, 'be bowed down, humbled': poor, afflicted, pressed low by others.

verses.translation_literal: [The] troubles of my heart have made wide; from my distresses bring me out.
verses.translation_dramatic: The troubles in my heart have spread, and spread, until there is no room left in me. Out of these narrow places, bring me out.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse plays on the Hebrew sense of 'narrow' and 'wide'. צָרוֹת, 'troubles', and מְצוּקוֹת, 'distresses', both come from roots of tightness and constriction; הִרְחִיבוּ means 'to make wide'. The irony is that the narrow things have become wide. Play the contradiction: it is the cramping that has taken up all the space in the heart. Then the plea 'bring me out' (הוֹצִיאֵנִי) is the cry of someone who has been squeezed, wanting out into open ground.

The grammar is disputed. Radak supplies an object: 'the troubles have widened their seat in my heart', the troubles have made themselves at home. Ibn Ezra, and the first view reported by Meiri, take the verb as intransitive: the troubles have grown wide, that is, many. Ibn Ezra also mentions and rejects the reading where 'heart' is the thing widened. KJV 'are enlarged' follows the intransitive sense, and is clear, but it blurs the sense of space that the Hebrew opposes to the narrowness of צָרוֹת. YLT's 'have enlarged themselves' is closer to Radak. The word 'heart' here is לֵבָב, the form with the doubled bet, the inner self, not just the seat of feeling.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to be wide'. Radak reads it as transitive with an implied object ('the troubles have widened their seat in my heart'); Ibn Ezra, and the first view in Meiri, read it as intransitive ('have become wide, many').
From the root 'to bind, be narrow'. The verse sets it against 'to make wide', a contrast the English 'troubles' cannot show. The word returns in the last verse of the psalm (צָרוֹתָיו).

verses.translation_literal: See my affliction and my toil, and lift off all my sins.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at what I carry: my misery, my weary labour. See it. And then take away every one of my sins.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb here is רְאֵה, 'see', and in the Bible God's seeing is never passive. When God 'sees' affliction (Exodus 3:7), he acts. So the psalmist asks God to look, expecting action to follow. The verse then asks for something harder: וְשָׂא, literally 'lift', 'carry off'. נָשָׂא with חֵטְא is the ordinary Hebrew idiom for forgiveness; it is the picture of a load being lifted off the person who has been bearing it. The KJV 'forgive' is right in meaning but loses the physical image. YLT's 'bear with' misses the direction: God takes the sin up and away, not along.

עָמָל is not just pain (KJV 'pain'). It is the trouble of labour, work that wears you out. The medieval commentators (Rashi, Radak, Malbim) join the two requests: the suffering the speaker has endured should count towards his atonement. That is their reading; the verse itself only puts them side by side.

philological_notes.note: 'Lift, carry off.' With חַטָּאת it is the standard idiom for forgiveness: the burden is lifted. Rashi and Malbim read the previous request as a reason for this one.
Toil, trouble that comes from labour; more than the KJV's 'pain'. Radak ties it to the toil of the wars.

verses.translation_literal: See my enemies, for they are many, and [with] hatred of violence they hate me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at my enemies, how many they have grown. They hate me, and the hatred is violence itself.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker repeats שׂנא, 'hate', as noun and then verb: 'hatred... they hate me.' Let the repetition build, it is the sound of a grievance being stated twice because once is not enough. The key word is חָמָס, 'violence', the wrong that cries out in the Hebrew Bible for redress (it is what fills the earth before the Flood, Gen 6:11). Rashi glosses it 'not in justice'; Radak, 'I did them no harm and they fight me'. Metzudat David reads it as 'they hate me as if I were a man of violence'. The hatred, then, is unjustified and turns into violence.

The KJV, 'they hate me with cruel hatred', does keep the repetition of noun and verb, so it should not be faulted for losing it. Its real loss is חָמָס: 'cruel' makes violence a description of temper, an adjective, where the Hebrew names a thing, a hatred whose substance is violence. The ASV and Webster copy this. YLT's 'with violent hatred' is nearer. BBE ('bitter is their hate of me') is the version that drops the repetition, and loses 'violence' as well.

philological_notes.note: 'Violence, wrong done by force', a legal and moral term, not just cruelty of mood. Here in the construct, 'hatred of violence', which is hatred that consists in violence, or an unjust hatred.
Noun and verb of the same root side by side (a figura etymologica), which intensifies the statement: they truly hate.

verses.translation_literal: Guard my life and rescue me; may I not be put to shame, for I have taken refuge in you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Keep my life. Pull me out of their hands. Do not let me stand ashamed, for it is in you that I have taken shelter.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three short commands, then the reason. Speak them fast, with the pressure of someone who has run out of time, and let 'for I have taken refuge in you' fall slowly as the only argument he has. 'Shame' (בוֹשׁ) is not only embarrassment. In a world where honour was public, to be put to shame is to be seen to be wrong and abandoned: if the one who trusted in God is overrun, God's name is dishonoured with him. Hence the force of the appeal.

נֶפֶשׁ is the whole living person, the life that can be threatened and taken, not a separate 'soul' as KJV's 'keep my soul' would suggest to a modern ear; Radak ties it to a fear of ambush ('they lie in wait for my life'). חָסִיתִי is physical: to flee to a rock or shadow for cover. KJV's 'I put my trust in thee' makes it a mental act; ASV's 'I take refuge in thee' is closer, though it turns a completed act into a present one. 'Let me not be ashamed' is a jussive: 'may I not be', a wish and a plea together.

philological_notes.note: 'I have taken refuge', a verb of fleeing to a shelter: a rock, a shadow, a wing. More concrete than 'trust'.
The living self, life, throat; what an enemy can take. Not an immortal 'soul' as a modern reader hears it.

verses.translation_literal: Integrity and uprightness, may they guard me, for I have waited for you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let blamelessness and honesty stand guard over me, for I have waited for you.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the poem speaks of two virtues as if they were two watchmen. תֹּם is wholeness, a life with nothing missing or hidden, and יֹשֶׁר is straightness, the quality of a road that does not bend. The same verb, נָצַר, is used of a guard watching a city. 'Let them guard me' therefore asks that his own honest dealing, standing beside God's protection, shield him from his enemies. The KJV 'preserve' is fine in sense but blurs the guard's watch; and BBE's 'for my clean and upright ways keep me safe' makes the virtues the reason instead of the guards.

קִוִּיתִיךָ is the verb for waiting with the cord stretched tight: קָוָה is related to קַו, a line or cord, so the waiting is a held tension, an expectation. The KJV 'wait on thee' reads as 'attend', as a servant attends a table; the Hebrew is 'I have hoped for you, I have strained toward you'. A stray יְהוָה stands after the verse end in this text, outside the acrostic and the line; it adds nothing to the sense.

philological_notes.note: To wait with tension, to hope; related to קַו, 'cord, line', hence a stretched, expectant waiting. Not 'wait on' as a servant does.
Integrity (wholeness) and uprightness (straightness), two qualities treated as guards. Metzudat David reads them as the deeds the speaker did, which now count in his favour.

verses.translation_literal: Redeem, God, Israel from all his troubles.
verses.translation_dramatic: Redeem Israel, O God. Out of every trouble that has closed around them, redeem them.
verses.directors_commentary:
After twenty-one verses of 'I' and 'me', the psalm ends on a different voice, for all of Israel. Metzudat David: 'not for myself alone do I pray, but for the whole of Israel'; Malbim hears the single man's prayer turning to the many who cannot rise to such detachment. Play the shift as a widening of the eyes, from his own narrow place to the people's. The verb פְּדֵה, 'redeem, ransom', is the word for buying back a person or property from a debt or bondage.

As the verse stands it is the only place in the psalm where the generic אֱלֹהִים is used as a vocative; the psalm has already said 'my God' (אֱלֹהַי, v2) and 'God of my salvation' (v5), and everywhere else it calls on YHWH or on no name at all. The change of title is striking; it may suit a prayer widened to include the nation, but that is my own conjecture, not a claim from the commentators. The verse also stands outside the alphabet that organizes the psalm: after the tav of v21 a final verse beginning with pe appears, a letter already used at v16; whether it is a later addition or a deliberate close on the nation is my own question to leave open. The word צָרוֹתָיו, 'his troubles', rhymes with צָרוֹת of v17, so the psalm opens and closes on the same cramped word. KJV 'out of all his troubles' is accurate; note that Hebrew speaks of Israel as a single 'he', as the name of the patriarch and the people at once.

philological_notes.note: The generic divine title, here in the vocative, the only absolute vocative in the psalm. The psalm elsewhere says 'my God' (v2) and 'God of my salvation' (v5).
'Ransom, redeem': to buy back a person or property from loss or bondage. Used for rescue from distress as well as from slavery.
